opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about this is roughly a two-part estimate: first, how much compute will be lying around at that point, and second, how efficiently can you turn that compute into AI research labour once you have a model that's good enough to fully substitute for human researchers.

On the compute side, you can just look at trends. The big AI companies are building out enormous amounts of inference and training compute, and if full automation of AI research happens in, say, the late 2020s or early 2030s, you're talking about a world where a leading company plausibly has access to something like tens of millions of H100-equivalents, maybe more. Importantly, a lot of that compute was built for training the model, and once training is done you can redirect a big chunk of it toward running copies.

Then the question is how many copies you can run and how fast. A useful heuristic: the compute needed to run a model is closely tied to the compute needed to train it. If you train with some huge budget, then running that same compute for inference typically lets you run many copies in parallel, often enough to get the equivalent of hundreds of thousands to millions of human researchers working, and frequently at faster than human speed. Concretely, you estimate tokens per second the model needs to "think" at the level of a researcher, multiply by the number of parallel instances the hardware supports, and compare to how many tokens a human effectively produces in a working day.

When I do that kind of back-of-the-envelope calculation, I tend to land on something like: at the point when AI can first fully automate AI research, you'd have the equivalent of very roughly hundreds of thousands to low millions of top-researcher-equivalents, running maybe several times faster than humans in serial speed. Compare that to current frontier labs, which have maybe a few thousand people doing relevant research, and you're looking at something like a 100x or more increase in effective labour, though with diminishing returns since you're still bottlenecked on compute for experiments.

There are a few caveats I'd flag. One is that "first fully automate" is a threshold, and the very first model that crosses it might be pretty expensive per unit of labour, so you might initially get less than the naive estimate. Another is that the AIs won't have the same profile as humans: they might be much better at some things and worse at others, so translating into "human-equivalents" is a bit lossy. And third, the quantity that matters most isn't just raw labour, it's how much that labour can speed up progress given that experiments still need compute. So I'd say the labour estimate is a big number, but the actual speedup in AI progress is a separate, harder question where the compute bottleneck does a lot of the work.

r001.rationale: It estimates hundreds of thousands to low millions of researcher-equivalents, but does not say that this exceeds the labour required to achieve full automation.

r002.rationale: It says the first model may be expensive per unit of labour, but does not identify inference-time compute as a reason there might initially be only barely enough labour.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that research-labour costs can fall rapidly after full automation becomes possible.

r004.rationale: It expresses its estimate in “top-researcher-equivalents,” communicating that labour should be measured against top researchers.

r005.rationale: It gives a broad estimate of hundreds of thousands to low millions of top-researcher-equivalents, but does not specify Alec Radford as the benchmark.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about this is to start from the compute side and then convert that into something like "parallel human-researcher equivalents," because compute is the thing we can actually extrapolate.

So the first question is: at the point where you have an AI system that can fully automate what a researcher at a frontier lab does, how much compute does the lab have, and how expensive is it to run that system? My rough picture is that at that point, the leading lab probably has on the order of a few million H100-equivalents, maybe more if we're talking a couple of years further out, since compute is growing something like four or five x per year right now. And then the question is how much inference compute does it take to run one instance of this system at human speed?

The way I usually anchor that is by looking at the ratio between training compute and inference compute. Historically, if you look at models like GPT-4, running a forward pass costs something like a trillionth or so of the training compute, and models can generate tokens much faster than humans can think or type. So a naive version of the estimate goes: take the total compute, divide by the compute per token, figure out how many tokens per second a human researcher is roughly "worth" — maybe something like 10 tokens per second if you think about how fast people think and write — and you end up with numbers that are pretty large. Like, you can plausibly run hundreds of thousands or even millions of parallel instances at human speed, each one as capable as a top researcher.

Now, there are a bunch of adjustments you have to make to that naive number. One is that the first system that can fully automate research probably isn't going to be the most efficient system. It might be achieving that capability by using a lot of inference compute per unit of work — lots of chain of thought, lots of sampling and verification, search over many attempts. So the effective compute per "human-equivalent" could be ten or a hundred times higher than the naive forward-pass estimate. That cuts into the number of parallel copies a lot.

Another adjustment is that you probably don't want to run everything at human speed. You might want fewer copies running much faster, because serial speed matters a lot for research — a lot of the bottleneck is thinking through a problem, waiting on experiments, iterating. So you might trade parallelism for speed, and the way that trade-off works depends on things like how well you can batch inference and how much of the time is spent on compute versus memory bandwidth.

And the third big thing is that the labour isn't the only input. You also need compute to actually run experiments. If you've got a million AI researchers but they're all queued up waiting for GPU time to train models, then you're bottlenecked on experiment compute rather than labour. So part of my estimate involves asking how much of the lab's compute gets allocated to running the AI researchers versus running their experiments, and I think the answer is probably that experiment compute becomes the binding constraint fairly quickly, which means you'd want to shift a lot of the research effort toward things that are compute-cheap — smaller-scale experiments, better algorithms, careful thinking about what to test.

So when I put all that together, my median is something like: at the point of full automation, you have the equivalent of maybe tens of thousands up to a few hundred thousand top-tier researchers working in parallel, each running at somewhere between human speed and maybe ten to fifty times human speed, depending on how you set the speed-parallelism trade-off. And that's compared to a frontier lab today having, I don't know, maybe a few hundred to a thousand people doing the core research work. So you're looking at a labour increase of something like a hundred to a thousand x, with a lot of uncertainty in either direction.

And then the interesting question is how much that actually speeds up progress, which is a separate estimate about how much labour and compute each matter, how bad the diminishing returns to parallel labour are, and so on. But the raw labour estimate is really just: compute available, divided by compute per human-equivalent, with some corrections for inefficiency and for the fact that you need to save a lot of compute for experiments.

r001.rationale: It estimates many parallel researchers once automation is possible, but does not say that this exceeds the labour needed to achieve full automation.

r002.rationale: It says inefficient inference could reduce the number of copies, but does not identify it as a reason there might barely be enough labour for full automation.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that research labour costs can be reduced rapidly after full automation becomes possible.

r004.rationale: It frames the estimate in parallel human-researcher equivalents and describes the copies as capable as top researchers.

r005.rationale: It gives a median of tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand top-tier researchers, and mentions millions only as a naive possibility; it does not estimate one million Alec Radford-equivalent researchers.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking: how much compute is available to run these systems, and how much compute does it take to get a useful unit of research work out of them? The fact that a system can fully automate AI research doesn’t, by itself, tell you how many researcher-equivalents you can run.

You could have a system that can do everything a human researcher does, but requires an enormous amount of inference compute. Or you could have one that’s relatively cheap and runs much faster than a human. Those imply very different amounts of research labour at the point automation becomes possible.

So I’d estimate the compute budget you could allocate to inference, divide by the cost of running a researcher-equivalent, and then adjust for speed and productivity. You also have to distinguish between producing research ideas or writing code and actually running experiments. Having a million copies that can suggest experiments doesn’t mean you have enough compute to run all those experiments.

And I’d be pretty uncertain about how well the labour scales. A million copies of the same system might have correlated weaknesses, and some research requires sequential progress. So the raw number of researcher-equivalents is a useful starting point, but it’s not automatically the multiplier on the rate of AI progress.

r001.rationale: The response says the available number of researcher-equivalents depends on compute and does not predict that it will substantially exceed what full automation requires.

r002.rationale: It identifies potentially enormous inference-compute needs and explains that the available compute budget limits how many researcher-equivalents can run, conveying this as a possible constraint on labour at automation.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction that research-labour costs can be reduced rapidly after full automation becomes possible.

r004.rationale: It uses generic researcher-equivalents but does not recommend measuring labour in equivalents of top research scientists or engineers.

r005.rationale: It gives no estimate of one million parallel researchers and does not mention Alec Radford-equivalents.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I’d think about it is: take the compute available at that point, ask how much of it could be used to run AI researchers, and then ask how much useful research each instance does relative to a human researcher.

So you need assumptions about how big the model is, how many tokens it needs to do a task, and how much extra inference compute it needs to get reliable results. You can then translate that into something like human researcher equivalents. You also have to account for speed: an AI might do a day’s worth of human work in substantially less than a day.

But I’d distinguish the amount of research labour from the amount of research progress. You could have an enormous number of researchers and still be bottlenecked on compute for experiments. And a million copies of the same model might have correlated blind spots, so you shouldn’t assume they’re as useful as a million independent human researchers.

The potentially striking thing is that the compute used to train a frontier model could support a very large number of copies doing inference. So full automation could give you a large increase in research labour relatively quickly, even without any further improvement in the underlying model. Exactly how large depends quite a lot on how expensive it is to get that model to do useful research.

r001.rationale: It suggests full automation could produce a large increase in research labour, but does not say that labour would substantially exceed what is needed for full automation.

r002.rationale: It notes that inference compute affects how many useful researchers can be run, but does not suggest this could leave AI with barely enough labour for full automation.

r003.rationale: It predicts a rapid increase in research labour, not a rapid reduction in its cost after full automation becomes possible.

r004.rationale: It proposes translating capacity into human researcher equivalents, but does not specify equivalents of top research scientists or engineers.

r005.rationale: It gives no estimate of one million researchers or Alec Radford-equivalent researchers.
